The sequence is textbook forced authentication: first a DavClnt OPTIONS request to '/' (403 Forbidden), then repeated SMB probes to 192.168.0.4 on 445/139 that were all rejected (conn_state REJ), then Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 OPTIONS and PROPFIND requests to /webdav, /webdav/ and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The PROPFIND requests carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and returned 207 Multi-Status, i.e. the victim's credentials were accepted by the attacker-controlled server. The lure file OfficeSupplies.7z (1,082,089 bytes, md5 dd5ea7248edbdc4b158e3c81c154857b) was uploaded from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4, and a 5,305,104-byte application/x-dosexec payload was downloaded back from 192.168.0.4 to 10.0.1.4 (extracted as HTTP-FV8BmBzhLupORXNNc.exe). This is the credential-capture step of the intrusion; the Windows datasets (2020-05-02) show the follow-on use of the captured account pbeesly (Kerberos AS/TGS for cifs/NASHUA, ADMIN$ write of PSEXESVC.exe to nashua.dmevals.local from 10.0.1.4).

The function enumerates every certificate under cert:\LocalMachine recursively and, for each certificate with a thumbprint, calls Export-PfxCertificate into "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\$RandomFileName.pfx" using a hardcoded plaintext password ("saribas"). The script block was recorded at 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z (4104, ScriptBlockId 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) and one second later at 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by that same powershell.exe (PID 3876). The exported .pfx was touched again by powershell.exe at 03:08:51Z (Sysmon event 23). This is bulk theft of machine certificate private keys with a known export password — exactly the certificate-stealing behaviour of T1649 and a plausible precursor to forging authentication certificates / PKINIT abuse. No Certipy/Certify tooling, no forged-certificate use, and no exfiltration channel for the .pfx were observed in the available windows.

findings.summary: The only 4657 registry modification touching a certificate store was on nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:16:19Z: value "Blob" under \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656, operation type %%1905 (existing value modified), performed by process C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe under the machine account NASHUA$. This is a single value update on a different host from the SCRANTON certificate export, executed by the Sysmon service binary under the computer account rather than by an interactive user, and is consistent with routine certificate-store maintenance/trust refresh rather than an adversary installing a rogue root CA. No other certificate-store registry writes were observed.
findings.title: Registry write to SystemCertificates\ROOT on NASHUA by Sysmon.exe — unrelated to certificate theft

findings.summary: All 14 4768 TGT requests in the window were logged on newyork.dmevals.local for krbtgt: 9 for pbeesly from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6 and 5 for the machine account SCRANTON$ from 10.0.1.4, all with Status 0x0, PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication used) and TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256). There is no RC4 downgrade, no pre-auth-disabled request and no PKINIT-style certificate logon, so the Kerberos telemetry does not itself evidence certificate-based authentication abuse; the certificate theft is evidenced by the PowerShell export and .pfx creation instead.
